text: # eSIM / Java Card VM Exploitation {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Overview (esim-javacard-exploitation)
text: ## Overview Embedded SIMs (eSIMs) are implemented as **Embedded UICC (eUICC)** smart-cards that run a **Java Card Virtual Machine (JC VM)** on top of a secure element. Profiles and applets can be provisioned *over-the-air* (OTA) through Remote SIM Provisioning (RSP) or OTA SMS, but reaching the VM still depends on a valid profile-management path and credentials. Where an attacker can install an untrusted applet, a VM memory-safety flaw can become code execution within the eUICC; the Kigen research used physical access and known keys, while the OTA path was simulated.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> This page describes a real-world full compromise of Kigen’s eUICC (Infineon SLC

title: HT: Attack Surface (esim-javacard-exploitation)
text: ## Attack Surface 1. **Remote Application Management (RAM)** eSIM profiles may embed arbitrary Java Card applets. Provisioning is performed with standard APDUs that can be tunnelled through SMS-PP (Short Message Service Point-to-Point) or HTTPS. If an attacker owns (or steals) the **RAM keys** for a profile, they can `INSTALL`/`LOAD` a malicious applet remotely.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 2. **Java Card byte-code execution** After installation, the applet executes inside the VM. Missing run-time checks allow memory corruption. ### 2024–2025 ecosystem changes * **TS.48 v7.x rollout** – the public GSMA TS.48 repository now deprecates all Generic Test Profile versions `v1`–`v6`, tells testers

title: HT: The Type-Confusion Primitive (esim-javacard-exploitation)
text: ## The Type-Confusion Primitive `getfield` / `putfield` are supposed to operate only on **object references**.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> In Kigen eUICC the instructions never validate whether the operand on the stack is an *object* or an *array* reference. Because an `array.length` word lives at the exact same offset as the first instance field of a normal object, an attacker can:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Create a byte-array `byte[] buf = new byte[0x100];` 2. Cast it to `Object o = (Object)buf;` 3. Use a crafted `putfield` field token to overwrite data at a field-derived offset in adjacent object state. 4. Use `getfield` to read memory after the corrupted state enables an out-of-bo

text: ## Cloning / Hijacking Demonstration Installing the same profile on **PHONE A** and **PHONE B** results in the Mobile Switching Centre routing incoming traffic to whichever device most recently registered. CVE-2025-22226 is a useful example of turning a **logically undersized HGFS payload** into an 8-byte host-heap disclosure: a privileged guest reaches `HGFileCopyCreateSessionCB`, the callback trusts fields beyond the operation's declared payload, and the leaked bytes return as an invalid session ID. Overwrites the mapped view with a fully relocated malicious PE but keeps the section object pointing to the benign image on disk. 3. text: ## Why asset relocations matter Many legacy game engines (Granny 3D, Gamebryo, etc.) load complex assets by: 1. Parsing a header and section table. 2. Allocating one heap buffer per section. 3. Applying relocation tables so that pointers embedded inside the section data get patched to the right target section + offset. When the relocation handler blindly trusts attacker-controlled metadata, every relocation becomes a potential arbitrary read/write primitive. So, if you send a `\x7f` ( `DELETE` -)it will **delete the previous character** of your exploit. In order to bypass this the **escape character `\x16` must be prepended to any `\x7f` sent.** This is terminal line-discipline behavior: the literal-next character (`VLNEXT`, commonly `Ctrl-V` or `0x16`) quotes the following byte instead of letting the TTY process it. title: HT: Image/Media Parsing Exploits (DNG/TIFF/JPEG) (common-exploiting-problems)
text: ## Image/Media Parsing Exploits (DNG/TIFF/JPEG) Malicious camera formats often ship their own bytecode (opcode lists, map tables, tone curves). When a privileged decoder fails to bound-check metadata-derived dimensions or plane indices, those opcodes become attacker-controlled read/write primitives that can groom the heap, pivot pointers, or even leak ASLR. Samsung's in-the-wild Quram exploit is a recent example of chaining a `DeltaPerColumn` bounds bug, heap spraying via skipped opcodes, vtable remapping, and a JOP chain to `system()`.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> {{#ref}} ../mobile-pentesting/android-app-pentesting/abusing-android-media-pipelines-image-parsers.md {{#endref}}

text: ## Back-end allocator: adjacency and same-size UAF replacement The back-end allocator (BEA) may split a larger free segment-tail chunk from its beginning, producing adjacent allocations of the same size. **Allocation order alone is not enough**: an existing exact-size free chunk or another suitable smaller free-list entry can be chosen instead. In Corelan's test, freeing a `0x300` tail chunk coalesced it with the remaining free space, but subsequent `0x100` requests reused pre-existing `0x100` and `0x198` free chunks rather than that large tail. text: ## Back-end coalescing for cross-size overlap When the replacement type is larger than the victim, arrange `[busy guard][predecessor][victim][busy guard]`. Free the victim and then its predecessor. BEA can coalesce them into one region beginning at the predecessor, so a larger allocation can be split from the front and extend into the old victim data. In the test, a `0x68` predecessor plus a `0x58` victim formed a free chunk with `0xc8` user bytes; a subsequent `0x80` allocation began at the predecessor address and covered the start of the former victim. text: ## LFH changes the reuse rules For the tested buckets, request 18 switched a size class from BEA to an LFH SubSegment. title: HT: Basic Information (integer-overflow-and-underflow)
text: ## Basic Information At the heart of an **integer overflow** is the limitation imposed by the **size** of data types in computer programming and the **interpretation** of the data. For example, an **8-bit unsigned integer** can represent values from **0 to 255**. If you attempt to store the value 256 in an 8-bit unsigned integer, it wraps around to 0 due to the limitation of its storage capacity. Similarly, for a **16-bit unsigned integer**, which can hold values from **0 to 65,535**, adding 1 to 65,535 will wrap the value back to 0. text: # VirtualBox VMSVGA COTable UAF Escape {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} This case study shows a useful hypervisor-exploitation pattern: a guest-controlled object remains referenced after destruction, two differently sized freed allocations are reclaimed with useful object types, and legitimate device commands are reused as typed read/write gadgets. The demonstrated target was VirtualBox's VMware SVGA-II 3D emulation on a Linux host.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The generic parts of the chain complement [Use After Free](libc-heap/use-after-free/), [Overwriting a freed chunk](libc-heap/overwriting-a-freed-chunk.md), [Write What Where 2 Exec](arbitrary-write-2-exec/), and [ROP & J

title: HT: Attack surface (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Attack surface The guest submits SVGA commands through a shared FIFO or a command buffer whose physical address is written to `SVGA_REG_COMMAND_LOW` and `SVGA_REG_COMMAND_HIGH`. DirectX contexts contain an `aCOTMobs[]` array of bound Memory Objects (MOBs), plus typed Context-Object Table pointers such as `cot.paSampler`. Binding a guest-backed MOB with `SVGA_3D_CMD_DX_SET_COTABLE` creates a host copy at `MOB->Gbo.pvHost`; both the MOB pointer and that host-buffer pointer then become reachable through the context.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Dangling COTable references (virtualbox-vmsvga-cotable-uaf-escape)
text: ## Dangling COTable references `SVGA_3D_CMD_DESTROY_GB_MOB` removes the selected MOB from the AVL tree and LRU list, destroys its Guest-Backed Object, and frees the `VMSVGAMOB`. The vulnerable lifetime transition did not verify whether any DX context still referenced that MOB. Consequently, both `aCOTMobs[type]` and the matching typed COT pointer could survive after the MOB and `pvHost` allocations were freed.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> The important audit rule is wider than this device: an object-table entry is an owning or borrowing reference even when the primary registry no longer contains the object. Destruction must reject a still-bound object or atomically invalidate every frontend

The sizes below are build-specific, but the allocation-role swap is reusable:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Define `MOB1` (`sizeof(VMSVGAMOB) == 0x68`). 2. The `0x68` MOB and `0x2170` backing buffer are freed, but context `2` retains stale aliases. 4. Bind another MOB with a `0x68` host buffer. text: ## Turning metadata corruption into disclosure For the initial leak, the exploit allocated six `0x68` MOBs, freed alternating entries, and bound the survivors with `0x68` backing buffers. It then set COTable element counters such as `cSampler` to `0xffffffff` without changing their pointers. The oversized logical count allowed a typed setter to pass bounds checks and overwrite an adjacent MOB's `Gbo.cbTotal`. Growing that COTable then copied more bytes than the original host buffer held back to guest memory, leaking adjacent heap objects, the `VBoxDD.so` base, and a `VMSVGAR3STATE` address. title: HT: Basic Information (array-indexing)
text: ## Basic Information Array-indexing vulnerabilities occur when a program fails to validate an index before using it to read or write an array. An out-of-bounds access may disclose memory, corrupt adjacent objects, or alter control data. The exploitation strategy depends on the array layout, the attacker's control over the index and value, and the binary's mitigations.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Overview (freebsd-ptrace-rfi-vm_map-prot_exec-bypass-ps5)
text: ## Overview This page documents a practical Unix/BSD usermode process/ELF injection technique on PlayStation 5 (PS5), which is based on FreeBSD. The method generalizes to FreeBSD derivatives when you already have kernel read/write (R/W) primitives.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> High level: - Patch the current process credentials (ucred) to grant debugger authority, enabling ptrace/mdbg on arbitrary user processes. - Find target processes by walking the kernel allproc list. - Bypass PROT_EXEC restrictions by flipping vm_map_entry.protection |= PROT_EXEC in the target’s vm_map via kernel data writes. - Use ptrace to perform Remote Function Invocation (RFI): suspend a thread, set registers to ca

title: HT: Kernel data-only primitives (freebsd-ptrace-rfi-vm_map-prot_exec-bypass-ps5)
text: ## Kernel data-only primitives ### Process discovery via allproc FreeBSD maintains a doubly-linked list of processes in kernel .data at allproc. With a kernel read primitive, iterate it to locate process names and PIDs:<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ```c struct proc* find_proc_by_name(const char* proc_name){ uint64_t next = 0; kernel_copyout(KERNEL_ADDRESS_ALLPROC, &next, sizeof(uint64_t)); // list head struct proc* proc = malloc(sizeof(struct proc)); do{ kernel_copyout(next, (void*)proc, sizeof(struct proc)); // read entry if (!strcmp(proc->p_comm, proc_name)) return proc; kernel_copyout(next, &next, sizeof(uint64_t)); // advance next } while (next); free(proc); return NULL; } void list_all_

title: HT: Bypassing RW-only user mappings: vm_map PROT_EXEC flip (freebsd-ptrace-rfi-vm_map-prot_exec-bypass-ps5)
text: ## Bypassing RW-only user mappings: vm_map PROT_EXEC flip Userland mmap may be constrained to PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE. FreeBSD tracks a process’s address space in a vm_map of vm_map_entry nodes (BST plus list). Each entry carries protection and max_protection fields:<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ```c struct vm_map_entry { struct vm_map_entry *prev,*next,*left,*right; vm_offset_t start, end, avail_ssize; vm_size_t adj_free, max_free; union vm_map_object object; vm_ooffset_t offset; vm_eflags_t eflags; vm_prot_t protection; vm_prot_t max_protection; vm_inherit_t inheritance; int wired_count; vm_pindex_t lastr; }; ``` With kernel R/W you can locate the target’s vm_map and set entry->protection |=

title: HT: Remote Function Invocation (RFI) with ptrace (freebsd-ptrace-rfi-vm_map-prot_exec-bypass-ps5)
text: ## Remote Function Invocation (RFI) with ptrace FreeBSD lacks Windows-style VirtualAllocEx/CreateRemoteThread. Instead, drive the target to call functions on itself under ptrace control:<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> 1. Attach to the target and select a thread; PTRACE_ATTACH or PS5-specific mdbg flows may apply. 2. Save thread context: registers, PC, SP, flags. 3. Write argument registers per the ABI (x86_64 SysV or arm64 AAPCS64), set PC to the target function, and optionally place additional args/stack as needed. 4. Single-step or continue until a controlled stop (e.g., software breakpoint or signal), then read back return values from regs. 5. Restore original context and continue. Use case

title: HT: Threaded stager and clean detach (freebsd-ptrace-rfi-vm_map-prot_exec-bypass-ps5)
text: ## Threaded stager and clean detach A minimal stager inside the target creates a new pthread that runs the ELF’s main and then triggers int3 to signal the injector to detach:<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> ```c int __attribute__((section(".stager_shellcode$1"))) stager(SCEFunctions* functions){ pthread_t thread; functions->pthread_create_ptr(&thread, 0, (void*(*)(void*))functions->elf_main, functions->payload_args); asm("int3"); return 0; } ``` - The SCEFunctions/payload_args pointers are provided by the loader/SDK glue. - After the breakpoint and detach, the payload continues in its own thread.

title: HT: Practical considerations (freebsd-ptrace-rfi-vm_map-prot_exec-bypass-ps5)
text: ## Practical considerations - Offsets and constants (allproc, ucred authority offset, vm_map layout, ptrace/mdbg details) are firmware-specific and must be updated per release. - Hypervisor protections force data-only kernel writes; do not attempt to patch CR0.WP or CR4.SMEP. - JIT memory is an alternative: some processes expose PS5 JIT APIs to allocate executable pages. The vm_map protection flip removes the need to rely on JIT/mirroring tricks. - Keep register save/restore robust; on failure, you can deadlock or crash the target.

title: HT: Inbound webhook receivers (webhook-security)
text: ## Inbound webhook receivers A webhook is an HTTP request that **another service** sends to the application when an event happens: a payment provider reports a successful payment, a code-hosting platform reports a push, a chat platform sends a slash command. The application exposes a public **receiver** URL such as `/webhooks/stripe` and acts on what it receives: it marks an order as paid, starts a deployment or creates a user. The receiver is reachable from the internet and usually has no session. The thing that proves the request comes from the real provider is a signature computed with a shared secret. Stripe warns that, without verification, an attacker can send fake events to trigger ac

title: HT: How common providers sign webhooks (webhook-security)
text: ## How common providers sign webhooks These schemes use HMAC-SHA256 with the **raw request body** in the signed input. Stripe and Slack also include a timestamp: - **GitHub** sends `X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<hex HMAC>`. GitHub tells receivers to use a constant-time comparison instead of `==`, and publishes a test vector: secret `It's a Secret to Everybody`, payload `Hello, World!`, signature `sha256=757107ea0eb2509fc211221cce984b8a37570b6d7586c22c46f4379c8b043e17`. The header is not present at all if no secret was configured for the webhook.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **Stripe** sends a `Stripe-Signature` header with the format `t=xxx,v1=yyy`.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> The timestam

title: HT: Receiver mistakes to test (webhook-security)
text: ## Receiver mistakes to test - **No verification at all**: any request with the right JSON shape is processed. - **Header presence only**: any value in `X-Hub-Signature-256` or `Stripe-Signature` is accepted. - **Optional verification**: the check runs only when a secret is configured. Stripe's own sample endpoint wraps verification in `if endpoint_secret`, and GitHub omits the signature header when no secret is set, so an empty secret in one environment silently disables the check.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> - **Verifying a transformed body**: Stripe and Slack require verification of the raw body before deserialization. Re-serializing JSON usually breaks legitimate verif

Send it in several versions and compare the response and the **side effect** (order status, deployment, created user): ```bash URL=https://target.tld/webhooks/github BODY='{"ref":"refs/heads/main","repository":{"full_name":"tester/test-repo"}}'

For timestamped schemes, check whether an event older than the tolerance is still accepted. 5. Change one field of a signed event (amount, status) **without** changing the signature. Acceptance means the signature does not cover the raw body, or is not checked. The receiver is vulnerable when any forged, replayed or modified event changes application state. title: HT: Basic Information (uuid-insecurities)
text: ## Basic Information Universally Unique Identifiers (UUIDs) are **128-bit numbers used to uniquely identify information** in computer systems. UUIDs are essential in applications where unique identifiers are necessary without central coordination. They are commonly used as database keys and can refer to various elements like documents and sessions.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> UUIDs are designed primarily for uniqueness, **not secrecy or authorization**. Some versions are predictable, and even a random UUID must not replace an access-control check. title: HT: Sandwich attack (uuid-insecurities)
text: ## Sandwich attack The "Sandwich Attack" is a specific type of attack that **exploits the predictability of UUID v1 generation in web applications**, particularly in features like password resets. text: ## Exploiting a subdomain takeover Subdomain takeover is essentially DNS spoofing for a specific domain across the internet, allowing attackers to set A records for a domain, leading browsers to display content from the attacker's server. title: HT: Basic Information (timing-attacks)
text: ## Basic Information The goal of a timing attack is to answer difficult questions or discover hidden functionality by **measuring consistent response-time differences between almost identical requests**. Traditionally this was very hard because the interesting server-side signal was drowned in network jitter and server noise. However, after the [**single-packet / synchronized-request techniques**](race-condition.md#http-2-single-packet-attack-vs.-http-1.1-last-byte-synchronization), it became practical to remove most transport noise from the equation and isolate tiny **server-side timing deltas**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> This page is focused on **server-side web timing oracles**. For **

title: HT: Making Timing Attacks Practical (timing-attacks)
text: ## Making Timing Attacks Practical A modern workflow is usually:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> 1. Build two requests that differ in **exactly one hypothesis** (header present/absent, valid/invalid hostname, duplicated parameter, valid/invalid structured payload, etc.). 2. Send both requests with the **same connection and the same release point** so the network path is shared. 3. **Alternate the order** of the pair to avoid bias caused by sticky ordering or server-side queue effects. 4. Repeat enough times to compare **paired deltas / medians**, not single measurements. 5. Tune the probe so one branch forces extra work such as **DNS resolution, cache misses, parsing, validation, logging, deser

title: HT: Discoveries (timing-attacks)
text: ## Discoveries ### Hidden Attack Surface Timing is excellent for discovering **hidden parameters, headers, cookies, or routes** even when the visible response looks identical. In the PortSwigger research, simply adding the right hidden input changed the timing by about **5ms**, which was enough to identify functionality that was otherwise invisible. This is now a natural fit for **Param Miner**.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> These time differences may appear because: - A **DNS lookup** is triggered. - A **different cache key** is used, turning a cache hit into a miss. - A hidden value reaches a **validation / parsing path**. - The application writes an **extra log entry** or throws an excepti

title: HT: Useful Tooling (timing-attacks)
text: ## Useful Tooling - **Param Miner**: good for timing-based discovery of hidden parameters/headers and for proxy-oriented timing checks. - **Turbo Intruder**: the timing templates alternate request order, repeat paired probes many times, and let you use cache-busting payloads such as `$randomplz` when needed. - **Burp Repeater - Send group in parallel**: great for quick proof-of-concept testing when you already know the two branches you want to compare. - **PacketSprinter**: useful when you want a UI around grouped parallel HTTP/2 requests and an easier way to compare synchronized responses side by side.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: What is it (server-side-javascript-injection)
text: ## What is it Server-side JavaScript injection (SSJI) happens when a Node.js application builds JavaScript code from user input and runs it. The code runs with the privileges of the server process, and no victim is needed: the attacker sends the request directly.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Look for calculators, formula or rule fields, filter and sort expressions, JSON parsed with `eval` instead of `JSON.parse`, and "custom script" options. Related pages: - MongoDB `$where` JavaScript: [NoSQL injection](nosql-injection.md). - Template engines and expression sandboxes: [SSTI](ssti-server-side-template-injection/). - Polluted objects reaching Node.js internals: [Prototype pollution to RCE](de

title: HT: Sinks and what the payload can reach (server-side-javascript-injection)
text: ## Sinks and what the payload can reach - **`eval()`**: Sullivan's example server parses the request body with `eval("(" + data + ")")`, so a body of `response.end('success')` returns `success` and proves execution.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Direct `eval` sees the local scope, so `require` and `response` are usable when they are in scope. - **`new Function()` / `Function()`**: functions created with the `Function` constructor only see the global scope.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Module-local names such as `require` are missing, so load modules through `process.mainModule.require` (deprecated alias of `require.main`) or `process.getBuiltinModule('child_process')` (Node.js 22.3.0 and 20.1

title: HT: Black-box detection (server-side-javascript-injection)
text: ## Black-box detection Change one thing at a time against a baseline request: 1. **Arithmetic and type probes**: `7*7` returning `49`, then `'7'+'7'` returning `77` and `[]+{}` returning `[object Object]`, which point to JavaScript. 2. **String break-out**: inside a quoted string, use `'+(7*7)+'` or `"+(7*7)+"`. A `SyntaxError` or `ReferenceError` in the response also shows that input reaches a JavaScript parser. 3. **Environment probes**: `typeof process`, `process.version` or `JSON.stringify(process.versions)`. 4. **Blind, time based**: `(function(){var t=Date.now();while(Date.now()<t+3000);})()` blocks the event loop for 3 seconds without any module. 5. **Blind, out of band**: `require('d

title: HT: Exploitation (server-side-javascript-injection)
text: ## Exploitation Sullivan's payloads list directories, read and write files, and run a written file:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```javascript response.end(require('fs').readdirSync('.').toString()) response.end(require('fs').readFileSync(filename)) require('fs').writeFileSync(filename, data, 'base64'); require('child_process').spawn(filename); ``` When only globals are reachable, use `process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id').toString()` or `process.getBuiltinModule('child_process').execSync('id').toString()`, and `JSON.stringify(process.env)` for secrets.<sup>[[3]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Business Logic Vulnerabilities (business-logic-vulnerabilities)
text: # Business Logic Vulnerabilities A business logic vulnerability is a flaw in the **rules** of the application, not in how it parses input. Every request can be well formed and free of injection, and the attacker still gets a result the designers did not want. Most logic flaws have their own page in HackTricks (see [Related pages](#related-pages)). This page covers automation of sensitive business flows and links to related logic flaws.

title: HT: Unrestricted access to sensitive business flows (business-logic-vulnerabilities)
text: ## Unrestricted access to sensitive business flows This is **OWASP API6:2023**. The problem is not a forbidden action but a legitimate flow with business value that can be **automated at scale** without control. OWASP's examples are buying the whole stock of a high-demand product to resell it (scalping), booking 90% of the seats of a flight with no cancellation fee and cancelling them later to force a price drop, and scripting registrations to collect referral credit in a ride-sharing app. Spamming a comment flow and reserving all available time slots are also listed.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> This is different from [rate limiting](rate-limit-bypass.md). text: ## `Referer` Header and Referrer Policy The HTTP `Referer` request header identifies the absolute or partial URL from which a resource was requested. Depending on the active referrer policy, it can include the referring origin, path, and query string, but not the URL fragment.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Sensitive Information Leakage Secrets in URL paths or query parameters can leak through browser history, logs, analytics, copied links, and the `Referer` header. title: HT: Mass Assignment (CWE-915) – Privilege Escalation via Unsafe Model Binding (mass-assignment-cwe-915)
text: # Mass Assignment (CWE-915) – Privilege Escalation via Unsafe Model Binding {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Mass assignment (a.k.a. insecure object binding / autobinding / over-posting) happens when an API/controller takes user-supplied JSON and directly binds it to a server-side model/entity without an explicit allow-list of fields. If privileged properties like roles, `isAdmin`, `status`, ownership fields, or backend-only processing options are bindable, any authenticated user can escalate privileges, tamper with protected state, or steer downstream code paths.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> This is a Broken Access Control issue (OWASP A01:2021). In API-centric applications it

title: HT: 1) Finding Mass Assignment (mass-assignment-cwe-915)
text: ## 1) Finding Mass Assignment Look for self-service endpoints that create or update objects:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> - `PUT/PATCH /api/users/{id}` - `PATCH /me`, `PUT /profile` - `PUT /api/orders/{id}` - `POST /api/checkout` - GraphQL mutations such as `updateProfile`, `editUser`, `saveCart`, `completeCheckout` Heuristics indicating mass assignment: - The response echoes server-managed fields (e.g., `roles`, `status`, `isAdmin`, `permissions`, `ownerId`, `tenantId`) even when you didn’t send them. - Client bundles contain role names/IDs or other privileged attribute names used throughout the app (`admin`, `staff`, `moderator`, `internal flags`), hinting bindable schema. - Backend serial

title: HT: 2) Exploitation – Role Escalation via Mass Assignment (mass-assignment-cwe-915)
text: ## 2) Exploitation – Role Escalation via Mass Assignment Once you know the bindable shape, include the privileged property in the same request.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup><sup>[[3]](#references)</sup> Example: set `roles` to `ADMIN` on your own user resource:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```http PUT /api/users/12934 HTTP/1.1 Host: target.example Content-Type: application/json { "id": 12934, "email": "user@example.com", "firstName": "Sam", "lastName": "Curry", "roles": [ { "id": 1, "description": "ADMIN role", "name": "ADMIN" } ] } ``` If the response persists the role change, re-authenticate or refresh tokens/claims so the app issues an admin-context session and shows privileged UI/endpoint

title: HT: 3) Hidden-Field Recon Beyond the Obvious (mass-assignment-cwe-915)
text: ## 3) Hidden-Field Recon Beyond the Obvious - Inspect minified JS bundles for role strings and model names; source maps may reveal DTO shapes. - Look for arrays/maps of roles, permissions, feature flags, workflow states, and checkout objects. Build payloads matching the exact property names and nesting. - Compare **GET** responses with **POST/PUT/PATCH** request bodies. If the response object contains `discount`, `credit`, `role`, `status`, or nested `internal` objects not present in the request, try replaying them in the write request. - Fetch machine-readable API docs if present (`/swagger.json`, `/v2/api-docs`, `/openapi.json`, GraphQL introspection). title: HT: 4) High-Value Abuse Patterns (mass-assignment-cwe-915)
text: ## 4) High-Value Abuse Patterns **Nested relation / tenant hijack** - Don’t stop at `role=admin`. In real APIs, reassigning `organizationId`, `accountId`, or `ownerId` is often more valuable because it can move your session, cart, invoice, API key, or ticket into another tenant. - Nested payloads are common: `{"profile":{"organizationId":7}}`, `{"order":{"owner":{"id":7}}}`, `{"user":{"team":{"id":1}}}`. **Business-flow tampering** - Checkout and billing APIs often return fields like `credit`, `chosen_discount`, `price`, `coupon`, `refundAmount`, or `approved`. title: HT: Quick protocol recap and attack surface (grpc-web-pentest)
text: ## Quick protocol recap and attack surface - Transport: gRPC‑Web speaks a browser‑compatible variant of gRPC over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 via a proxy (Envoy/APISIX/grpcwebproxy/etc.). Only unary and server‑streaming calls are supported. - Content-Types you will see: - application/grpc-web (binary framing) - application/grpc-web-text (base64-encoded framing for HTTP/1.1 streaming) - Framing: every message is prefixed with a 5‑byte gRPC header (1‑byte flags + 4‑byte length). title: HT: What are WebSockets (websocket-attacks)
text: ## What are WebSockets WebSocket connections are established through an initial **HTTP** handshake and are designed to be **long-lived**, allowing for bidirectional messaging at any time without the need for a transactional system. This makes WebSockets particularly advantageous for applications requiring **low latency or server-initiated communication**, such as live financial data streams. ### Establishment of WebSocket Connections A detailed explanation on establishing WebSocket connections can be accessed [**here**](https://infosecwriteups.com/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-cswsh-ce2a6b0747fc). title: HT: WebSocket as a transport for messaging/queue protocols (MQTT, STOMP, AMQP) (websocket-attacks)
text: ## WebSocket as a transport for messaging/queue protocols (MQTT, STOMP, AMQP) A WebSocket is just a **bidirectional transport** — it doesn't say anything about the protocol spoken on top of it. Many real-time applications (chat widgets, live support, IoT dashboards, trading frontends, notification systems) **tunnel a message-broker / pub‑sub protocol over the WebSocket** instead of inventing their own framing. When you find a WebSocket, do not assume it is a bespoke JSON API: it may be a direct pipe into a **message queue / broker**, which means topic subscription, wildcard abuse and broken authorization become in scope. title: HT: Prevention (reverse-tab-nabbing)
text: ## Prevention Use explicit `rel="noopener"` on untrusted `<a>`, `<area>`, and `<form>` navigations with any target that can create a new context. title: HT: Defensive Cheat-Sheet (updated 2025) (nosql-injection)
text: ## Defensive Cheat-Sheet (updated 2025) 1. Strip or reject keys that start with `$`; if Express is in front of Mongo/Mongoose, sanitize `req.body`, `req.query`, and `req.params` before they reach the ORM. 2. Disable server-side JavaScript on self-hosted MongoDB (`--noscripting` or `security.javascriptEnabled: false`) so `$where` and similar JS sinks are unavailable. 3. Prefer `$expr` and typed query builders instead of `$where`. 4. Validate data types early (Joi/Ajv/Zod) and disallow arrays or objects where scalars are expected to avoid `[$ne]` tricks. 5. title: HT: HTTP Connection Request Smuggling (http-connection-request-smuggling)
text: # HTTP Connection Request Smuggling {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} **HTTP connection request smuggling** is a **connection-state / routing** problem rather than a classic CL.TE/TE.CL parser discrepancy. The bug appears when a front-end decides **where a connection is allowed to go only once**, then silently reuses that same TCP/TLS connection for later requests with a different `Host` or `:authority`.<sup>[[1]](#references)[[2]](#references)</sup> If you need the classic length-confusion variants, see [HTTP Request Smuggling / HTTP Desync Attack](http-request-smuggling/README.md) and [Request Smuggling in HTTP/2 Downgrades](http-request-smuggling/request-smuggling-in-http-2-d

title: HT: Connection-State Attacks (http-connection-request-smuggling)
text: ## Connection-State Attacks ### First-request Validation When routing requests, reverse proxies often depend on the **Host** header (or **`:authority`** in HTTP/2) to decide the destination back-end server and whether that destination is allowed. A recurring bug class is that this whitelist is **only enforced on the first request on a connection**. After that, the front-end trusts the connection itself instead of re-validating each request: ```http GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: allowed-external-host.example GET /admin HTTP/1.1 Host: internal-only.example ``` This turns connection reuse into an SSRF-like primitive against **internal virtual hosts**, admin panels, debug

title: HT: Browser-Powered Connection-State Abuse (2022-2025) (http-connection-request-smuggling)
text: ## Browser-Powered Connection-State Abuse (2022-2025) The most practical modern variant is **browser-powered** exploitation. A victim first opens a legitimate connection to an attacker-controlled or attacker-triggered origin, and the browser later **reuses or coalesces** that connection for a different authority.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Coalescing preconditions worth checking For HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, prioritize targets where several hostnames share the same edge infrastructure: - The certificate presented on the existing connection is valid for **both** the attacker-controlled hostname and the target hostname. - For classic HTTP/2 coalescing, browsers commonly require the hostnames to

title: HT: Related State-Transition Abuse: `h2c` Upgrade Tunnelling (http-connection-request-smuggling)
text: ## Related State-Transition Abuse: `h2c` Upgrade Tunnelling A closely related bug appears when a front-end forwards **`Upgrade: h2c`** and, after the `101 Switching Protocols`, stops inspecting the traffic and simply tunnels bytes to the back end. In practice, the proxy may enforce routing / ACLs only on the **initial HTTP/1.1 request**, after which the attacker speaks raw clear-text HTTP/2 directly to the internal service. ```http GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: public.example Connection: Upgrade, HTTP2-Settings Upgrade: h2c HTTP2-Settings: AAMAAABkAAQCAAAAAAIAAAAA ``` This is worth testing on reverse proxies that support upgrade-style tunnelling or permissive `proxy_pass` rules. ---

title: HT: Tooling (http-connection-request-smuggling)
text: ## Tooling - **HTTP Request Smuggler** (Burp) – useful for **connection-state probes**, hidden-HTTP/2 testing, browser-powered desync work, and modern parser-discrepancy detection. - **`http2smugl`** – purpose-built for finding **HTTP/2 → HTTP/1.1 downgrade** smuggling paths and related request poisoning opportunities. - **`smugglefuzz`** – a **Go-based** downgrade smuggling scanner with customizable gadget lists and fast bulk probing. - **`h2cSmuggler`** – focuses on `Upgrade: h2c` tunnelling mistakes that bypass front-end ACLs. ---

title: HT: Mitigations (http-connection-request-smuggling)
text: ## Mitigations - Re-validate **`Host` / `:authority` on every request and every HTTP/2 stream**, not just once per socket. - Keep **internal and external hostnames** on separate certificates / origin sets / Alt-Svc advertisements when possible. - Return **`421 Misdirected Request`** when a reused connection is not authoritative for the new origin. - Strip or hard-code **`Upgrade: h2c`** at the edge unless it is explicitly required. - Where feasible, avoid reusing a single privileged upstream connection across unrelated tenants or trust zones. ---

title: HT: **Reusing Reset Token** (account-takeover)
text: ## **Reusing Reset Token** Should the target system allow the **reset link** (or an equivalent **magic link**) to be **reused**, efforts should be made to **find more reset links** using tools such as `gau`, `wayback`, or `scan.io`.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> Also verify whether the artifact still works **after an email change** or when redeemed from a **second browser/device**.

title: HT: **Pre Account Takeover** (account-takeover)
text: ## **Pre Account Takeover** 1. The victim's email should be used to sign up on the platform, and a password should be set (an attempt to confirm it should be made, although lacking access to the victim's emails might render this impossible). 2. One should wait until the victim signs up using OAuth and confirms the account. 3. It is hoped that the regular signup will be confirmed, allowing access to the victim's account.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: **CORS Misconfiguration to Account Takeover** (account-takeover)
text: ## **CORS Misconfiguration to Account Takeover** If the page contains **CORS misconfigurations** you might be able to **steal sensitive information** from the user to **takeover his account** or make him change auth information for the same purpose:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> {{#ref}} cors-bypass.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: **CSRF to Account Takeover** (account-takeover)
text: ## **CSRF to Account Takeover** If the page is vulnerable to CSRF, you may be able to make the **user modify their password, email, or authentication settings** and then access the account:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> {{#ref}} csrf-cross-site-request-forgery.md {{#endref}}

title: HT: **XSS to Account Takeover** (account-takeover)
text: ## **XSS to Account Takeover** If you find XSS in an application, you may be able to steal cookies, local-storage data, or page content that enables account takeover:<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> {{#ref}} xss-cross-site-scripting/ {{#endref}} - Attribute-only reflected payloads on login pages can hook `document.onkeypress`, exfiltrate keystrokes through `new Image().src`, and steal credentials without submitting the form. title: HT: What is CORS? (cors-bypass)
text: ## What is CORS? Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) standard **enables servers to define who can access their assets** and **which HTTP request methods are permitted** from external sources.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup> A **same-origin** policy mandates that a **server requesting** a resource and the server hosting the **resource** share the same protocol (e.g., `http://`), domain name (e.g., `internal-web.com`), and **port** (e.g., 80). title: HT: Exploitable misconfigurations (cors-bypass)
text: ## Exploitable misconfigurations It has been observed that the setting of `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` to **`true`** is a prerequisite for most **real attacks**. This setting permits the browser to send credentials and read the response, enhancing the attack's effectiveness. Without this, the benefit of making a browser issue a request over doing it oneself diminishes, as leveraging a user's cookies becomes unfeasible.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Exception: Exploiting Network Location as Authentication An exception exists where the victim's network location acts as a form of authentication. This is because scripts need to be able to be included from different domains. This vulnerability allows an attacker to access and read any content that was included using the script tag. title: HT: Phone Number Injections (phone-number-injections)
text: # Phone Number Injections {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Applications often treat a phone number as a simple string even though a `tel` URI may contain semicolon-delimited parameters such as `ext`, `isub`, and `phone-context`.[[1]](#references) If an application accepts these suffixes but different components validate, store, render, or forward them inconsistently, the suffix may reach an injection sink or bypass controls based on exact string comparison. Test for XSS, SQL injection, SSRF, parser discrepancies, and downstream telephony issues only where the application's data flow makes the corresponding sink plausible.[[2]](#references)

title: HT: Basic Information (client-side-path-traversal)
text: ## Basic Information A client-side path traversal (CSPT), also called **on-site request forgery (OSRF)**, occurs when attacker-controlled data is inserted into a URL path used by client-side code. By injecting dot segments such as `../`, an attacker can make the victim's browser send an authenticated request to a different path on the same origin. The request may carry cookies, JavaScript-added authorization headers, or a client certificate, depending on how the application constructs it.<sup>[[5]](#references)[[7]](#references)</sup> Typical sources (data you control) include route parameters, stored values, and UI-controlled path fragments:<sup>[[7]](#references)[[8]](#references)</sup> -

text: # Application-Layer DoS (Unrestricted Resource Consumption) Application-layer resource exhaustion occurs when **cheap requests make the server do disproportionate work** or trigger paid third-party actions. Repeated requests can then slow the service or produce a large bill. OWASP classifies this as API4:2023 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption) and notes that crafted requests with parameters that control the number of returned resources, combined with response status, time and length analysis, should identify the issue.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> For GraphQL batching, aliases, directives and depth limits, check [DoS in GraphQL](../network-services-pentesting/pentesting-web/graphql.md#dos-i

title: HT: How to test safely (application-layer-dos)
text: ## How to test safely The goal is to prove that a limit is missing, not to take the target down. Use a test account, avoid peak hours and stop as soon as the trend is clear: 1. Pick one request and record its normal **response time and size**. 2. Increase one value step by step (for example `10`, `100`, `1000`, `10000`) and record time and size at each step. 3. If time or size grows with the value and no limit is observed, record the tested range; this suggests a missing or overly high cap, but does not prove that no cap exists. A few sequential measurements are enough. Do not send the largest values in parallel. 4. Report the input, the measured growth and the extrapolation instead of causi

title: HT: Unbounded page size, ranges and arrays (application-layer-dos)
text: ## Unbounded page size, ranges and arrays Look for parameters that control **how much** the server processes or returns: `limit`, `size`, `page_size`, `per_page`, `count`, `max`, `top`, `first`, `take`, `depth`, date ranges (`from`/`to`), `ids=1,2,3,...` lists and JSON arrays. ```http GET /api/v1/orders?page=1&per_page=100000 HTTP/1.1 GET /api/v1/reports?from=1970-01-01&to=2100-01-01 HTTP/1.1 POST /api/v1/users/lookup {"ids":[1,2,3, ... 50000]} ``` OWASP lists "number of records per page to return in a single request-response" among the limits that must exist. text: ## Paid actions and cost amplification Some requests cost the owner money each time: SMS, emails or phone calls, biometric checks, paid APIs, or large downloads served from origin. OWASP lists the third-party providers' spending limit as a required limit.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **Per-request paid actions**: in OWASP's first scenario, a `forgot password` call makes the backend ask an SMS provider that charges $0.05 per message. title: HT: Hash collision DoS (HashDoS) (application-layer-dos)
text: ## Hash collision DoS (HashDoS) Web frameworks often put request parameters (query string, form fields, JSON keys) in a hash table. If the hash function is not randomized, an attacker can send many keys with the **same hash**, so every insert becomes slow and one large request burns a lot of CPU. CERT/CC VU#903934 describes this for language implementations that do not randomize their hash functions or limit key collisions, where "specially-crafted POST form data" can cause a DoS on some web application servers.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup> The fixes included randomized hash functions and limits on the number of request parameters. title: HT: Session-scoped authorization state reuse (403-and-401-bypasses)
text: ## Session-scoped authorization state reuse Some applications record a completed verification as a boolean in the session, then let a different endpoint rely on that flag. After legitimately passing the check for one resource, test whether the same flag incorrectly authorizes a different user, object, or workflow. This is a second-order authorization/state-reuse flaw, not merely an IDOR.<sup>[[6]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Thread-local identity leakage across batched RPC calls (403-and-401-bypasses)
text: ## Thread-local identity leakage across batched RPC calls A batched RPC endpoint may run several methods in sequence on one worker thread. In the reported Archibus DWR case, a pre-authentication method loaded a privileged core-user session into a thread-local `ContextStore`; a later workflow method in the same batch used that stored identity rather than the unauthenticated caller. The workflow's group-membership check therefore evaluated the core account. This is different from a persistent session flag: the trust boundary is crossed between calls inside one request. title: HT: Stale authorization after role, membership or key changes (403-and-401-bypasses)
text: ## Stale authorization after role, membership or key changes An authorization check is only correct if it uses the **current** permissions of the caller. Many applications instead keep permissions that were valid when a credential was issued. After an admin removes a member from a team, downgrades a role, disables a user or revokes an integration, the old credentials of that user still work. OWASP ASVS 5.0 requirement 8.3.2 asks to "verify that changes to values on which authorization decisions are made are applied immediately". When this is not possible (for example with self-contained tokens), it asks for compensating controls that alert and reverse the action, and it notes that this does

title: HT: ASP.NET Core static files before authorization (403-and-401-bypasses)
text: ## ASP.NET Core static files before authorization In ASP.NET Core applications, `UseStaticFiles()` commonly runs before `UseAuthorization()`. Files served at that point are public even if the app has a fallback policy that requires authentication. `MapStaticAssets` endpoints in .NET 9 and later are subject to endpoint authorization when the authorization middleware runs; check for `ShortCircuit()` or anonymous endpoint metadata before assuming they are protected. Identify which path serves the asset before drawing conclusions.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> - Request a known document or user-uploaded file anonymously, then with an authenticated session. title: HT: Basic Information (dependency-confusion)
text: ## Basic Information Dependency Confusion (a.k.a. substitution attacks) happens when a package manager resolves a dependency name from an unintended, less-trusted registry/source (usually a public registry) instead of the intended private/internal one. This typically leads to the installation of an attacker-controlled package. Common root causes: - Typosquatting/misspelling: Importing `reqests` instead of `requests` (resolves from public registry). - Non-existent/abandoned internal package: Importing `company-logging` that no longer exists internally, so the resolver looks in public registries and finds an attacker’s package. - Version preference across multiple registries: Importing an inte

title: HT: Exploitation (dependency-confusion)
text: ## Exploitation > [!WARNING] > In all cases, the attacker only needs to publish a malicious package with the same name as the dependency your build resolves from a public registry. Installation-time hooks (e.g., npm scripts) or import-time code paths often give code execution. ### Misspelled & Inexistent If your project references a library that isn’t available in the private registry, and your tooling falls back to a public registry, an attacker can seed a malicious package with that name in the public registry. Your runners/CI/dev machines will fetch and execute it. ### Unspecified Version / “Best-version” selection across indexes Developers frequently leave versions unpinned or allow wide

title: HT: AWS Fix (dependency-confusion)
text: ## AWS Fix This vulnerability was found in AWS CodeArtifact (read the details in this blog post). AWS added controls to mark dependencies/feeds as internal vs external so the client won’t fetch “internal” names from upstream public registries.<sup>[[2]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Finding Vulnerable Libraries (dependency-confusion)
text: ## Finding Vulnerable Libraries In the original post about dependency confusion the author looked for thousands of exposed manifests (e.g., `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, lockfiles) to infer internal package names and then published higher-versioned packages to public registries.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Practical Attacker Playbook (for red teams in authorized tests) (dependency-confusion)

title: HT: Defender Playbook (what actually prevents confusion) (dependency-confusion)
text: ## Defender Playbook (what actually prevents confusion) High-level strategies that work across ecosystems: - Use unique internal namespaces and bind them to a single registry. - Avoid mixing trust levels at resolution time. Prefer enforcing these in CI and developer environments. ### JavaScript/TypeScript (npm, Yarn, pnpm) - Use scoped packages for all internal code and pin the scope to your private registry. - Keep installs immutable in CI (npm lockfile, `yarn install --immutable`). .npmrc (project-level) ```

title: HT: XML Injection (Tag Injection) (xml-injection)
text: # XML Injection (Tag Injection) {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: What is XML injection (xml-injection)
text: ## What is XML injection Applications often insert user input into an XML document that the server builds itself, such as a record in an XML store or a request to a backend service. If XML metacharacters are not encoded, the input adds markup to that document.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> This is not [XXE](xxe-xee-xml-external-entity.md). Tag injection uses ordinary elements, comments and CDATA sections, so it still works when entities and DTDs are disabled. It changes the **structure** of the document: it adds, overrides or hides fields that the consumer later trusts.

title: HT: Detection (xml-injection)
text: ## Detection Send each metacharacter alone in every value that might reach server-side XML and look for parser errors, 500 responses or changed behaviour:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - `'` and `"` break a value placed inside an attribute delimited by that quote. - `<` (for example `foo<`) makes an element value malformed. - `<!--` starts a comment that is never closed. - `&` starts an entity reference, and `&foo` is neither terminated nor defined. - `]]>` closes a CDATA section when the value is wrapped in `<![CDATA[...]]>`. Compare with the encoded form (`<`) to confirm that the server does not escape the input.

title: HT: Exploitation (xml-injection)
text: ## Exploitation ### Adding an element Close the current element, add the element you want, and reopen the element you closed so the server's own markup stays valid. In the OWASP example, a registration form builds a `<user>` node in which `userid` sets the privileges, and the e-mail value is inserted raw:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ``` E-mail: tony@evil.net</mail><userid>0</userid><mail>tony@evil.net ``` The node then has two `userid` elements, and the consumer probably uses the last one, `0` (the admin ID). If the document is validated against a DTD or schema that allows only one `userid`, the duplicate is rejected.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Hiding the original element with a comme

title: HT: **Password Reset Token Leak Via Referrer** (reset-password)
text: ## **Password Reset Token Leak Via Referrer** - The HTTP referer header may leak the password reset token if it's included in the URL. This can occur when a user clicks on a third-party website link after requesting a password reset. - **Impact**: Potential account takeover if a third party receives and redeems the leaked reset token. - **Exploitation**: To check if a password reset token is leaking in the referer header, **request a password reset** to your email address and **click the reset link** provided. **Do not change your password** immediately. Instead, **navigate to a third-party website** (like Facebook or Twitter) while **intercepting the requests using Burp Suite**. Inspect the

title: HT: **Password Reset Poisoning** (reset-password)
text: ## **Password Reset Poisoning** - Attackers may manipulate the Host header during password reset requests to point the reset link to a malicious site. - **Impact**: Leads to potential account takeover by leaking reset tokens to attackers.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup> Back ends sometimes trust the HTTP `Host` field when constructing absolute links. If a password-reset email uses an attacker-supplied host, requesting a reset for a victim can send a token-bearing link through an attacker-controlled domain. Also test forwarded-host fields, duplicate Host handling, and absolute-form request targets at each proxy hop.<sup>[[17]](#references)</sup> > [!WARNING] > A user click may not be necessary:

title: HT: **Password Reset By Manipulating Email Parameter** (reset-password)
text: ## **Password Reset By Manipulating Email Parameter** Attackers can manipulate the password reset request by adding additional email parameters to divert the reset link.<sup>[[5]](#references)</sup><sup>[[6]](#references)</sup><sup>[[7]](#references)</sup><sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> - Add attacker email as second parameter using & ```php POST /resetPassword [...] email=victim@email.com&email=attacker@email.com ``` - Add attacker email as second parameter using %20 ```php POST /resetPassword [...] email=victim@email.com%20email=attacker@email.com ``` - Add attacker email as second parameter using | ```php POST /resetPassword [...] email=victim@email.com|email=attacker@email.com ``` - Add at

title: HT: **Changing the Email and Password of Any User Through API Parameters** (reset-password)
text: ## **Changing the Email and Password of Any User Through API Parameters** - Attackers can modify email and password parameters in API requests to change account credentials.<sup>[[9]](#references)</sup> ```php POST /api/changepass [...] ("form": {"email":"victim@email.tld","password":"12345678"}) ``` - **Mitigation Steps**: - Ensure strict parameter validation and authentication checks. - Implement robust logging and monitoring to detect and respond to suspicious activities.

title: HT: **No Rate Limiting: Email Bombing** (reset-password)
text: ## **No Rate Limiting: Email Bombing** - Lack of rate limiting on password reset requests can lead to email bombing, overwhelming the user with reset emails.<sup>[[10]](#references)</sup> - **Mitigation Steps**: - Implement rate limiting based on IP address or user account. - Use CAPTCHA challenges to prevent automated abuse.

title: HT: **Find out How Password Reset Token is Generated** (reset-password)
text: ## **Find out How Password Reset Token is Generated** - Understanding the pattern or method behind token generation can lead to predicting or brute-forcing tokens. Some options: - Based Timestamp - Based on the UserID - Based on email of User - Based on Firstname and Lastname - Based on Date of Birth - Based on Cryptography - Also request several reset links in parallel and compare them. Identical tokens, deterministic increments, or "one-time" links that remain valid after first use usually indicate a race condition or a state machine bug. - **Mitigation Steps**: - Use strong, cryptographic methods for token generation. - Ensure sufficient randomness and length to prevent predictability. -

title: HT: **Guessable UUID** (reset-password)
text: ## **Guessable UUID** - If UUIDs (version 1) are guessable or predictable, attackers may brute-force them to generate valid reset tokens. Check: {{#ref}} uuid-insecurities.md {{#endref}} - **Mitigation Steps**: - Use GUID version 4 for randomness or implement additional security measures for other versions. - **Tools**: Use [guidtool](https://github.com/intruder-io/guidtool) for analyzing and generating GUIDs.

title: HT: **Response Manipulation: Replace Bad Response With Good One** (reset-password)
text: ## **Response Manipulation: Replace Bad Response With Good One** - Manipulating HTTP responses to bypass error messages or restrictions.<sup>[[11]](#references)</sup> - **Mitigation Steps**: - Implement server-side checks to ensure response integrity. - Use secure communication channels like HTTPS to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

title: HT: **Using Expired Token** (reset-password)
text: ## **Using Expired Token** - Testing whether expired tokens can still be used for password reset. - Check both the final reset endpoint and any intermediate "validate token" endpoint. Some applications reject the token on the UI step but still accept it on the JSON/API step that actually changes the password. - **Mitigation Steps**: - Implement strict token expiration policies and validate token expiry server-side.

title: HT: **Race / Reuse of One-Time Reset Tokens** (reset-password)
text: ## **Race / Reuse of One-Time Reset Tokens** - Some applications invalidate reset tokens only after the password update finishes, or only in one worker/process. This makes supposedly one-time links reusable when the same token is submitted concurrently. - Practical checks: - Open the same reset link in two browsers and submit both almost at the same time. - Send two `POST /reset` requests in parallel with the same token but different passwords. - Complete the password change once, then replay the exact final request before following any redirect chain. - If two different passwords are accepted or the same token works twice, you likely found a race condition in token invalidation. - **Mitigat

title: HT: **Brute Force Password Reset Token** (reset-password)
text: ## **Brute Force Password Reset Token** - Attempting to brute-force the reset token using tools like Burpsuite and IP-Rotator to bypass IP-based rate limits. - **Mitigation Steps**: - Implement robust rate-limiting and account lockout mechanisms. - Monitor for suspicious activities indicative of brute-force attacks.

title: HT: Email Injections (email-injections)

title: HT: Mutable Claims Attack (oauth-to-account-takeover)
text: ## Mutable Claims Attack In OAuth, the sub field uniquely identifies a user, but its format varies by Authorization Server. To standardize user identification, some clients use emails or user handles. However, this is risky because: - Some Authorization Servers do not ensure that these properties (like email) remain immutable. - In certain implementations—such as **"Login with Microsoft"**—the client relies on the email field, which is **user-controlled by the user in Entra ID** and not verified. - An attacker can exploit this by creating their own Azure AD organization (e.g., doyensectestorg) and using it to perform a Microsoft login. - Even though the Object ID (stored in sub) is immutable

title: HT: Client Confusion Attack (oauth-to-account-takeover)
text: ## Client Confusion Attack In a **Client Confusion Attack**, an application using the OAuth Implicit Flow fails to verify that the final access token is specifically generated for its own Client ID. An attacker sets up a public website that uses Google’s OAuth Implicit Flow, tricking thousands of users into logging in and thereby harvesting access tokens intended for the attacker’s site. If these users also have accounts on another vulnerable website that does not validate the token's Client ID, the attacker can reuse the harvested tokens to impersonate the victims and take over their accounts.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Scope Upgrade Attack (oauth-to-account-takeover)
text: ## Scope Upgrade Attack The **Authorization Code Grant** type involves secure server-to-server communication for transmitting user data. However, if the **Authorization Server** implicitly trusts a scope parameter in the Access Token Request (a parameter not defined in the RFC), a malicious application could upgrade the privileges of an authorization code by requesting a higher scope. After the **Access Token** is generated, the **Resource Server** must verify it: for JWT tokens, this involves checking the JWT signature and extracting data such as client_id and scope, while for random string tokens, the server must query the Authorization Server to retrieve the token’s details.<sup>[[4]](#re

title: HT: Redirect Scheme Hijacking (oauth-to-account-takeover)
text: ## Redirect Scheme Hijacking In mobile OAuth implementations, apps use **custom URI schemes** to receive redirects with Authorization Codes. However, because multiple apps can register the same scheme on a device, the assumption that only the legitimate client controls the redirect URI is violated. On Android, for instance, an Intent URI like `com.example.app://` oauth is caught based on the scheme and optional filters defined in an app’s intent-filter. Since Android’s intent resolution can be broad—especially if only the scheme is specified—an attacker can register a malicious app with a carefully crafted intent filter to hijack the authorization code. This can **enable an account takeover*

text: ## Conditionals - **`Last-Modified`** is a response validator containing the origin server's selected modification time for the representation. Clients can send that value in `If-Modified-Since` or `If-Unmodified-Since`; coarse or synthetic timestamps and clock behavior can affect its reliability.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> - **`If-Modified-Since`** asks for the representation only if it changed after the supplied date; otherwise a successful conditional `GET`/`HEAD` normally receives `304`. **`If-Unmodified-Since`** instead requires that the resource has not changed and otherwise normally produces `412` for a state-changing request.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> - **`If-Match`** requires a

title: HT: Range requests (special-http-headers)
text: ## Range requests - **`Accept-Ranges`**: Indicates if the server supports range requests, and if so in which unit the range can be expressed. `Accept-Ranges: <range-unit>` - **`Range`**: Requests part of a representation. For example, `Range: bytes=80-100` asks for bytes 80 through 100 and can produce `206 Partial Content`. Removing `Accept-Encoding` often makes byte offsets easier to reason about.<sup>[[8]](#references)</sup> - If an attacker can inject a `Range` request header, a partial response may isolate reflected JavaScript or other bytes that were harmless in the complete representation. Exploitability depends on browser behavior, content type, and intermediary caching. - **`If-Range

title: HT: Message body information (special-http-headers)
text: ## Message body information - **`Content-Length`:** The size of the resource, in decimal number of bytes. - **`Content-Type`**: Indicates the media type of the resource - **`Content-Encoding`**: Used to specify the compression algorithm. - **`Content-Language`**: Describes the human language(s) intended for the audience, so that it allows a user to differentiate according to the users' own preferred language. - **`Content-Location`**: Indicates an alternate location for the returned data. These fields are often routine, but differences on a resource protected by `401` or `403` can become an oracle for hidden content.\ For example a combination of **`Range`** and **`Etag`** in a HEAD request

title: HT: Controls (special-http-headers)
text: ## Controls - **`Allow`**: This header is used to communicate the HTTP methods a resource can handle. For example, it might be specified as `Allow: GET, POST, HEAD`, indicating that the resource supports these methods. - **`Expect`**: Utilized by the client to convey expectations that the server needs to meet for the request to be processed successfully. A common use case involves the `Expect: 100-continue` header, which signals that the client intends to send a large data payload. The client looks for a `100 (Continue)` response before proceeding with the transmission. This mechanism helps in optimizing network usage by awaiting server confirmation.

title: HT: What is Clickjacking (clickjacking)
text: ## What is Clickjacking In a clickjacking attack, a **user** is **tricked** into **clicking** an **element** on a webpage that is either **invisible** or disguised as a different element. This manipulation can lead to unintended consequences for the user, such as the downloading of malware, redirection to malicious web pages, provision of credentials or sensitive information, money transfers, or the online purchasing of products.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ### Prepopulate forms trick Sometimes it is possible to **prepopulate form fields with query parameters when loading a page**. An attacker may combine this behavior with clickjacking so the victim only has to press the submit button. ###

title: HT: Strategies to Mitigate Clickjacking (clickjacking)
text: ## Strategies to Mitigate Clickjacking ### Client-Side Defenses Scripts executed on the client side can perform actions to prevent Clickjacking: - Ensuring the application window is the main or top window. - Making all frames visible. - Preventing clicks on invisible frames. - Detecting and alerting users to potential Clickjacking attempts. However, these frame-busting scripts may be circumvented: - **Browsers' Security Settings:** Some browsers might block these scripts based on their security settings or lack of JavaScript support. - **HTML5 iframe `sandbox` Attribute:** An attacker can neutralize frame buster scripts by setting the `sandbox` attribute with `allow-forms` or `allow-scripts`

text: ## Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Explained **Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** lets an attacker trigger actions through a victim's authenticated browser session. title: HT: Web Vulnerabilities Methodology (web-vulnerabilities-methodology)
text: # Web Vulnerabilities Methodology {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}} Every web pentest has both obvious and hidden attack surfaces. This page is a checklist for confirming that the major vulnerability classes and application components have been reviewed. For request replay and identity-differential authorization testing, see [Burp Suite Intruder and Session Switcher](burp-suite.md#multi-session-authorization-testing-with-session-switcher). Many production DApps are hybrid systems with a normal web frontend, RPC provider, indexer, and centralized API around the on-chain component; “decentralized” therefore describes an architectural property, not a guarantee of security or the absence of servers.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> For blockchain and transaction concepts before assessing the on-chain component, see [Blockchain and Crypto-Currencies — Basic Concepts](../blockchain/blockchain-and-crypto-currencies/README.md#basic-concepts). title: HT: What is content spoofing (content-spoofing-text-injection)
text: ## What is content spoofing **Content spoofing** (also called content injection, arbitrary text injection or virtual defacement) happens when an attacker can make a trusted site show content chosen by the attacker. The victim sees the message on the real domain, so they trust it. It is mainly a **phishing and social-engineering** primitive.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> There are two forms:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **Text injection**: the application encodes the input correctly, so no markup or XSS is possible, but the page still shows the text that the attacker put in the URL or in a stored field. - **HTML injection**: the application inserts the input as HTML without running JavaScrip

title: HT: Text injection in web pages (content-spoofing-text-injection)
text: ## Text injection in web pages Look for pages where a **message comes from a parameter** instead of from a fixed list of messages. Typical places are error pages, login messages (`?error=`, `?msg=`), "not found" pages that echo the path, status texts and search pages that print the query inside a sentence. The OWASP example controls a stock recommendation shown by the trusted site:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text http://vulnerablesite/suggestions.php?stockid=123&stockrecommendation=We+Really+Recommend+You+Sell+This+Stock+Now ``` How to test it: 1. Find every parameter and path segment that is shown as a sentence in the page. 2. Replace it with a long, realistic message (a phone number,

title: HT: HTML injection in web pages (content-spoofing-text-injection)
text:
## HTML injection in web pages With HTML injection the attacker can draw a fake login form on the real domain. The OWASP example sends the credentials to the attacker's server:[[1]](#references) ```text http://target/vulnerable.php?name=

Please Enter Your Username and Password to Proceed:

Username:
Password:
``` Even under a strict CSP, an injected form can still abuse password autofill, as explained in [CSP form-action](content-security-policy-csp-bypass/#form-action).

title: HT: HTML and link injection in e-mail bodies (content-spoofing-text-injection)
text: ## HTML and link injection in e-mail bodies Many applications put user-controlled values into **e-mails sent by the service itself**. Examples are invitations ("*Alice invited you to the organization X*"), share notifications, comments and mentions, receipts and support tickets. These e-mails come from the real service. If the value is inserted into the HTML template without encoding, the attacker controls part of a trusted e-mail sent to any address they choose. An invitation e-mail is one example: when an organization name is inserted without HTML encoding, a user who controls that name can make the recipient see an attacker-chosen link such as `click me`

title: HT: Impact (content-spoofing-text-injection)
text: ## Impact Content spoofing alone does not execute JavaScript. Its impact depends on the context: injected content that is not visually different from valid content can be used in social engineering, and unescaped input may enable stronger HTML-based attacks.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> Impact grows when the content is shown on a sensitive page (login, payment, account settings), when it is stored and shown to many users, or when it is sent by the service to arbitrary e-mail addresses.

text: # Reflected File Download (RFD) {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: What is RFD (reflected-file-download)
text: ## What is RFD In a **Reflected File Download** attack the victim follows a link to a **trusted domain** and the browser **downloads** the response as a file. The attacker controls part of the file **content** (reflected input) and its **name and extension** (from the URL). If the victim opens the file, for example `setup.bat`, Windows runs the reflected content as commands. Every browser indicator shows that the file came from the trusted site.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> RFD works even when the reflected value is **correctly escaped** for JSON or JavaScript. The file is not interpreted by the browser, but by another program such as `cmd.exe` or Windows Script Host.<sup>[[1]](#references)<

title: HT: Detecting RFD (reflected-file-download)
text: ## Detecting RFD ### 1. Reflected input that breaks into shell context Look for reflection in parameters, error messages (APIs that echo the invalid value or path), stored data fetched by id, and JSONP callbacks.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> JSON escapes `"` as `\"`, but batch files escape with `^`, not with `\`. So in a `.bat` file the backslash is just a character and the `"` still closes the quoted string. After that, batch command separators let you run commands. An unencoded line feed also starts a new command line:<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> ```text {"a":"rfd\"&calc&","b":"b"} & runs both commands {"a":"rfd\"||calc||","b":"b"} || runs calc when the previous command fails {"a":"rfd\"&

title: HT: Mitigations (reflected-file-download)
text: ## Mitigations - Return `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=1.txt` (or another fixed, safe name) on API responses that users do not need to open directly.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Use exact URL mapping, so extra path segments or path parameters return 404.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Encode instead of escaping, and do not echo invalid input in API errors.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - Use an allowlist for JSONP callbacks, require a custom header or CSRF token for API calls, and add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: RSQL Injection (rsql-injection)
text: # RSQL Injection {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: What is RSQL? (rsql-injection)
text: ## What is RSQL? RSQL is a query language designed for parameterized filtering of inputs in RESTful APIs. Based on FIQL (Feed Item Query Language), originally specified by Mark Nottingham for querying Atom feeds, RSQL stands out for its simplicity and ability to express complex queries in a compact and URI-compliant way over HTTP. This makes it an excellent choice as a general query language for REST endpoint searching.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: Overview (rsql-injection)
text: ## Overview RSQL injection occurs when an application exposes attacker-controlled RSQL filters without constraining the permitted fields, relations, and operators. Unlike [SQL injection](sql-injection/README.md) or [LDAP injection](ldap-injection.md), RSQL normally builds read filters rather than raw database statements; the typical impact is unauthorized data access, enumeration, or authorization bypass. Modification or deletion requires an application-specific endpoint that applies attacker-controlled filters to a mutation.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup>

title: HT: How does it work? (rsql-injection)
text: ## How does it work? RSQL allows you to build advanced queries in RESTful APIs, for example: ```bash /products?filter=price>100;category==electronics ``` This translates to a structured query that filters products with price greater than 100 and category “electronics”. If the application does not correctly validate user input, an attacker could manipulate the filter to execute unexpected queries, such as: ```bash /products?filter=id=in=(1,2,3);delete_all==true ``` An attacker can also extract sensitive information through Boolean query oracles and nested relationship filters.

title: HT: Risks (rsql-injection)
text: ## Risks - **Exposure of sensitive data:** An attacker can retrieve information that should not be accessible.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> - **Data modification or deletion:** Possible when a mutation endpoint uses the injected filter to select records for update or deletion; filter injection alone is generally read-only. - **Privilege escalation:** Manipulation of identifiers that grant roles through filters to trick the application by accessing with privileges of other users. - **Evasion of access controls:** Manipulation of filters to access restricted data. - **Impersonation or IDOR:** Modification of identifiers between users through filters that allow access to information and resourc

title: HT: HTTP/2 Protocol-Level DoS (CONTINUATION Flood, MadeYouReset) (http2-protocol-dos)
text: # HTTP/2 Protocol-Level DoS (CONTINUATION Flood, MadeYouReset) {{#include ../banners/hacktricks-training.md}}

title: HT: Basic Information (http2-protocol-dos)
text: ## Basic Information HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection. Each request is a **stream**, and everything travels as binary frames (`HEADERS`, `CONTINUATION`, `DATA`, `RST_STREAM`, `WINDOW_UPDATE`, `PRIORITY`, `SETTINGS`, `GOAWAY`...). The attacks on this page do not need an application bug. They abuse how an HTTP/2 front-end (reverse proxy, load balancer or application server) handles frames, so that cheap frames from the client cost the server CPU or memory. The client-side stream cancellation attack (Rapid Reset) and the nginx settings that make it worse are covered in [nginx](../network-services-pentesting/pentesting-web/nginx.md#http2-rapid-reset-resilience-cve-2023-44

title: HT: CONTINUATION Flood (http2-protocol-dos)
text: ## CONTINUATION Flood A header block is sent either as a single `HEADERS` frame with `END_HEADERS`, or as a `HEADERS` frame without `END_HEADERS` followed by `CONTINUATION` frames, where the last one sets `END_HEADERS`.<sup>[[1]](#references)</sup> In a CONTINUATION flood the client opens a request and then keeps sending `CONTINUATION` frames that **never** set `END_HEADERS`. Implementations that do not limit the number or total size of these frames keep decoding or buffering a header block that never ends.<sup>[[2]](#references)[[3]](#references)</sup> Depending on the implementation the impact is:<sup>[[2]](#references)[[4]](#references)</sup> - **CPU exhaustion**: the server HPACK-decodes

title: HT: MadeYouReset (server-triggered resets) (http2-protocol-dos)
text: ## MadeYouReset (server-triggered resets) MadeYouReset works like Rapid Reset, but the **server** sends the `RST_STREAM`. A stream that has been reset no longer counts toward `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`, while affected implementations keep processing the request in the backend. The attacker can therefore keep an unbounded number of requests in flight on one connection.
